To superimpose means to place or lay one thing directly on top of another, in such a way that both remain visible or recognizable at the same time. The defining feature of this word is layering without replacing — the bottom thing doesn't disappear; it stays, with the new thing resting over it.

Imagine a photograph of a city street. Now imagine placing a transparent sheet over it — one with a hand-drawn grid on it. You're now looking at both: the photograph beneath and the grid on top, occupying the same space simultaneously. The act of placing that grid over the photograph is superimposing one onto the other.

The verb is almost always paired with the prepositions on, onto, or over:

  • "She superimposed the new image onto the old one."
  • "The editor superimposed the title text over the opening scene."
  • "He superimposed one city map on another to compare the two layouts."

The structure is usually: superimpose [Thing A] on/onto/over [Thing B] — where Thing A is what you're placing, and Thing B is what it's being placed upon.
Where you'll encounter this word in real life

Photography and film. When two images are blended together — say, a person's silhouette appearing over a sunset — one image has been superimposed on the other. When subtitles or a news ticker appear over live video, they are superimposed.

Maps and data visualization. A mapmaker might superimpose a layer of rainfall data over a plain map of a country, so you see the geography and the weather information together.

Geometry. When checking whether two shapes are perfectly identical (congruent), you can mentally superimpose one shape onto the other to test if every point lines up exactly.

Architecture and engineering. Designers frequently superimpose one plan or blueprint over another to compare layouts or spot conflicts between, say, the electrical system and the plumbing.
The figurative use — where the word becomes especially powerful

You don't need physical objects to superimpose. The word is used heavily in a non-physical, mental or interpretive sense — and this is just as valid and common.

Example 1:
"Walking back into her childhood home after twenty years, she found herself superimposing old memories onto every corner of the house."

Here, she isn't physically placing anything. Her mind is layering the past over the present — she sees the actual room in front of her and her memories of it at the same time, both visible at once.

Example 2:
"The critic argued that the director had superimposed his personal politics onto a story that was never meant to carry them."

The director has laid his own interpretation over the existing story. The story itself is still there, but now it's also carrying a meaning that wasn't originally in it. Both layers are present.

The figurative use always preserves the core logic of the word: something is being deliberately placed over something else, and both coexist.
How it differs from similar words

Replace — When you replace something, you remove the original and put something new in its place. Superimposing never removes anything; both things stay. This is a crucial difference.

Overlap — Overlap is more neutral and describes a spatial relationship: two things share some area or space. Superimpose is more active — it describes the deliberate act of placing one thing upon another, with intention.

Overlay — This is the word closest to superimpose and is often interchangeable. The subtle difference: overlay tends to focus on the layer itself as a thing (a text overlay, a color overlay), while superimpose tends to emphasize the action of placing one thing over another. In practice, the two words can usually be swapped without changing the meaning in most sentences.
The one idea to hold onto

Whenever you encounter "superimpose," picture two things occupying the same space — one placed deliberately over the other — with neither disappearing. It is always about coexistence, layering, and the deliberate act of placing one thing upon another, whether that's images, maps, shapes, memories, or ideas.
